summary: Describes a scheme to packetize an H.261 video stream for transport using RTP over any underlying protocol. It also defines the SDP parameters for H.261 and a media type registration. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: H.261 is an old video format. This says how to cut its video into small packets that can be sent over the internet and put back together.

questions: what is the rtp payload format for h.261
what do sbit and ebit mean in h.261 rtp
how does h.261 recover from packet loss
subtitle: How to chop H.261 videoconference video into RTP packets that survive loss on the Internet.

tldr.problem: H.261 video was designed for fixed-rate ISDN circuits, but its hierarchical bit stream cannot be decoded without header information that may sit in a lost packet.
tldr.mechanism: The stream is split at macroblock boundaries, and each RTP packet carries a small H.261 header repeating the state needed to decode it on its own: bit positions, GOB number, macroblock address predictor, quantizer and motion vector data.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2032, deprecates the H.261-specific FIR and NACK control packets, and adds SDP and media type parameters for H.261.

facts.label: Minimum INTRA refresh
facts.value: Each MB at least every 132 times sent

today: RFC 4587 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2006. It obsoletes RFC 2032 and is not marked as obsoleted or updated by any later RFC in the metadata for this site.

sections.title: Why H.261 Needs a Payload Format
sections.content:
ITU-T Recommendation H.261 specifies the encoding used by ITU-T-compliant video-conference codecs. It was originally specified for fixed-data rate ISDN circuits, but experiments cited by the RFC showed it can also be used over packet-switched networks such as the Internet.

This memo specifies how to encapsulate an H.261 video stream in RTP. It obsoletes RFC 2032 and updates the video/h261 media type that was registered in RFC 3555.
sections.eli5: An old video-call format was made for phone-style lines. This RFC teaches it how to travel as packets over the Internet instead.

sections.title: How H.261 Video Is Organized
sections.content:
H.261 video is a sequence of frames. Each frame is divided into Groups of Blocks (GOBs), each GOB holds 3 lines of 11 macroblocks (MBs), and each MB covers a 16x16 pixel area. Changed blocks are compressed with a discrete cosine transform, quantized and Huffman encoded.

The hierarchy matters for packetization. To decode the GOBs you need the frame header, and to decode the macroblocks you need the GOB header. Sent naively over UDP, you would have to receive every packet of an image to decode any of it.

The RFC therefore sends the output of the Huffman encoding directly. It does not carry the 512-bit ISDN frames, because protection against bit errors can be obtained by other means, and it does not multiplex audio with video, since UDP and RTP already provide that.
sections.eli5: A picture is cut into tiles, and tiles are grouped into bigger tiles. To read a small tile you need the label of the group it belongs to, which is why a lost label causes trouble.

sections.title: Packetization Design
sections.content:
A whole image, or even one GOB, can be too large for one packet, so the macroblock is the unit of fragmentation. Packets must start and end on an MB boundary, so an MB is never split across packets. Several MBs may share a packet, which is recommended to cut packet rate and overhead. The bit stream cannot be fragmented between a GOB header and MB 1 of that GOB.

So that each packet can be processed independently after a loss, some state is copied into every packet: the GOB number in effect, the macroblock address predictor, the quantizer value in effect and the reference motion vector data. Because compressed MBs rarely fill whole octets, two 3-bit fields, SBIT and EBIT, say how many bits are unused in the first and last octet.

For hardware codecs, the cheapest approach is to packetize whole GOBs that fit in a packet, found via the GOB-start pattern. When a GOB is too large the packetizer must parse the Huffman coding to fragment at MB level, which the RFC recommends as more efficient.
sections.eli5: Every parcel gets a sticky note repeating what you need to know to open it alone. Parcels are only ever cut between whole tiles, never through the middle of one.

sections.title: RTP Header Use and the H.261 Header
sections.content:
The H.261 header follows the RTP header. The RTP payload type is not assigned by this document; the RTP profile assigns one or a dynamic payload type is chosen. The RTP timestamp uses a 90-kHz clock and is the same on all packets of one image. The marker bit MUST be set to one in the last packet of a frame, so a receiver need not wait for the next frame's start code.

The H.261 header has these fields: SBIT (3 bits), EBIT (3), I (1), V (1), GOBN (4), MBAP (5), QUANT (5), HMVD (5) and VMVD (5). The I and V flags are hints that tell decoders whether the stream is INTRA-only and whether motion vectors are used. They cannot change during the stream, and a conforming implementation can always set V=1 and I=0. The H.261 stream SHALL be used without BCH error correction and without error correction framing.
sections.eli5: The sticky note has a few small boxes: how many bits to skip at each end, which group the parcel is in, and some numbers for rebuilding the picture.

sections.title: Dealing with Packet Loss
sections.content:
On the Internet most loss comes from congestion, and UDP gives the sender no feedback, so recovery is up to the codec. H.261 compresses by differences from earlier frames (INTER-frame coding), so after a loss parts of the image may stay corrupt until the affected macroblocks are sent in INTRA-frame mode.

The RFC lists three mitigations: use only INTRA-frame coding with conditional replenishment of changed MBs; raise the INTRA refresh rate when receivers see loss (H.261 requires an MB to be INTRA coded at least every 132 times it is sent); or request an INTRA refresh after detecting loss, which is the fastest repair and works well when there are few decoders.

The H.261-specific control packets FIR and NACK from RFC 2032 SHALL NOT be used. Refreshes are requested instead with RTCP feedback messages from RFC 4585, or with application commands such as the H.245 FastUpdateRequest.
sections.eli5: If a parcel gets lost, the picture can look broken for a while. The fix is to send fresh whole pictures more often, or to ask for one when something goes missing.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The video/H261 media type has no required parameters and three optional ones. CIF and QCIF take an integer from 1 to 4 and give the maximum frame rate for that resolution as 29.97 divided by the value. D signals support for still image graphics under H.261 annex D, and its value SHALL be 1 if supported.

In SDP the media name MUST be video, the encoding name MUST be H261 and the clock rate MUST be 90000. The optional parameters go in the a=fmtp line. In offer/answer, implementations SHALL specify at least one picture size, and parameters offered first are the most preferred. A receiver that gives no picture size is assumed to follow RFC 2032, and it is RECOMMENDED to assume it can receive QCIF with MPI=1.
sections.eli5: When two video callers say hello, they can say which picture sizes they like and how fast they can handle them, listing their favourite first.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Packets are subject to the security considerations of RFC 3550 and the applicable RTP profile such as RFC 3551. Confidentiality comes from encryption, and SRTP may provide both encryption and integrity protection. Because compression is applied end to end, encryption is done after compression and the two do not conflict.

The RFC also warns of a denial-of-service threat: an attacker can inject pathological datagrams that are costly to decode. H.261 is vulnerable because an attacker can craft packets containing frames that affect decoding of future frames, so data origin authentication and integrity protection of at least the RTP packet is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Someone could send tricky packets that make the receiver work too hard, so the RFC suggests checking that packets really come from the right sender.

fields.name: SBIT
fields.desc: Most significant bits to ignore in the first data octet.

fields.name: EBIT
fields.desc: Least significant bits to ignore in the last data octet.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: 1 if the stream has only INTRA-frame coded blocks.

fields.name: V
fields.desc: 0 if motion vectors are not used; 1 if they may be.

fields.name: GOBN
fields.desc: GOB number in effect at the start of the packet.

fields.name: QUANT
fields.desc: Quantizer value in effect before this packet.

viz.caption: WAYS TO RECOVER FROM LOSS (RFC 4587 SECTION 5)

items.title: INTRA only
items.text: Use only INTRA-frame coding with conditional replenishment of changed macroblocks.

items.title: Adaptive refresh
items.text: Raise the INTRA refresh rate when receivers measure significant loss.

items.title: Request a refresh
items.text: Ask the coder for an INTRA-coded image after a loss; fastest repair.
